name: Ipratropium
summary: Short-acting inhaled antimuscarinic that blocks vagally mediated bronchoconstriction; a standard bronchodilator for COPD and an add-on in acute asthma.
mechanism: Competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M1–M3), reducing cholinergic bronchomotor tone and mucus hypersecretion.

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Low systemic absorption after inhalation (~7–28% of delivered dose)

dosing.adult: MDI: 2–4 puffs (17–21 mcg/puff) 4 times daily; nebulized: 500 mcg every 6–8 h; intranasal: 2 sprays per nostril 2–3 times daily
dosing.maxDose: MDI up to 12 puffs/day; nebulized up to 2 mg/day

safety.pregnancy: Inhaled use gives minimal systemic exposure; generally considered low risk
contraindications: Soy or peanut allergy (Atrovent HFA contains soy lecithin)
warnings: Narrow-angle glaucoma — avoid eye contact (can precipitate angle closure)
Urinary retention, especially with prostatic hyperplasia
Paradoxical bronchospasm — discontinue if it occurs
monitoring: Anticholinergic symptoms (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary hesitancy)
safety.overdose: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, tachycardia, blurred vision) — supportive care

indications: Add-on to a SABA in acute severe asthma
Rhinorrhea of allergic rhinitis or the common cold (intranasal)
clinicalPearls: Quaternary ammonium compound — does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so central anticholinergic effects are minimal
Nebulized ipratropium added to salbutamol is standard for acute severe asthma
good: Bronchodilation with negligible systemic anticholinergic toxicity
bad: Acute asthma as monotherapy (use with a SABA); narrow-angle glaucoma or significant urinary retention
